cases.name: an-integer-literal-past-the-domain-is-a-double
cases.description: Where the whole-number domain ends. A literal wider than signed 64-bit is a DOUBLE, not a refusal — so these two different numbers compare equal, both having rounded to the same double. That is deliberate and pinned elsewhere: the shared case `expressions-math-2/nan-and-infinity-behave-as-ieee-says` compares 1/0 against 100000000000000000000 on purpose, and refusing the literal would break it. Only ARITHMETIC that leaves the domain is refused, which the case below shows.
cases.config: <tdc><env count="2" seed="s" local="en"><sequence name="V"><gen type="text" value="x" if="10000000000000000000 == 10000000000000000001"/></sequence></env><block><line><data>[${{V}}]</data></line></block></tdc>

cases.name: the-largest-integer-still-fits
cases.description: The other side of the boundary: the two largest values the domain holds compare correctly, and nothing is refused.
cases.config: <tdc><env count="2" seed="s" local="en"><sequence name="V"><gen type="text" value="x" if="9223372036854775807 == 9223372036854775806"/></sequence></env><block><line><data>[${{V}}]</data></line></block></tdc>

cases.name: a-fraction-is-still-a-fraction
cases.description: The rule is about WHOLE numbers. A literal written with a point is a fraction on purpose and stays a double.
cases.config: <tdc><env count="2" seed="s" local="en"><sequence name="V"><gen type="text" value="x" if="3.14 > 3"/></sequence></env><block><line><data>[${{V}}]</data></line></block></tdc>

cases.name: arithmetic-that-leaves-the-domain-passes-check
cases.description: The other side of the same boundary. Both operands are inside the domain and only the RESULT is not, so `check` cannot see it: this config validates and the run refuses it with `integer overflow: 9223372036854775808 is outside the signed 64-bit range`. Recorded here so the silence at validation time is deliberate rather than discovered.
cases.config: <tdc><env count="2" seed="s" local="en"><sequence name="V"><gen type="text" value="x" if="9223372036854775807 + 1 > 0"/></sequence></env><block><line><data>[${{V}}]</data></line></block></tdc>

cases.name: a-misspelled-function-in-expr
cases.description: expr= is the same little language as if=, and the expressions page promises all four homes read the same way. Until this case existed only if= was handed to the checker, so a misspelled function passed check and killed the run with a bare unknown function — no code, no line.
cases.config: <tdc><env count="2" seed="s" local="en"><sequence name="A"><gen type="number" value="1..9"/></sequence><sequence name="B"><gen type="formula" expr="besselj(A)"/></sequence></env><block><line><data>${{B}}</data></line></block></tdc>

cases.name: a-misspelled-function-in-a-distribution-parameter
cases.description: The fourth home. A parameter written as an expression reaches the same evaluator, so it has to be refused by the same list.
cases.config: <tdc><env count="2" seed="s" local="en"><sequence name="A"><gen type="number" value="1..9"/></sequence><sequence name="B"><gen type="number" distribution="normal" mean="besselj(A)" sd="1"/></sequence></env><block><line><data>${{B}}</data></line></block></tdc>

cases.name: a-misspelled-function-in-a-pool-filter
cases.description: The third home. The pool checks knew which FIELDS a filter reads and nothing about whether the expression was runnable at all.
cases.config: <tdc><env count="2" seed="s" local="en"><pool name="P" count="3"><sequence name="price"><gen type="number" value="1..9"/></sequence></pool><sequence name="R"><gen type="pool" value="P" filter="besselj(price) > 0"/></sequence></env><block><line><data>${{R.price}}</data></line></block></tdc>
